summary:
Malacca stands under the federal framework of Malaysia. Sections 377A and 377B of the Federal Penal Code 1936 criminalise same-sex sexual activity with a maximum penalty of twenty years' imprisonment plus whipping, and section 377D, covering outrages on decency, criminalises gross indecency in terms the Human Dignity Trust records as usable against transgender people. These provisions are not limited to Malaysian citizens and reach visitors present in Malacca.

The Sharia layer reaches Malacca as well. Every one of Malaysia's thirteen states maintains an enactment criminalising cross-dressing or 'a man posing as a woman', carrying up to three years' imprisonment, a fine of RM5,000 and six strokes of caning. These offences apply to Muslims only, are enforced by state Islamic religious departments, and contain no legal definition of what constitutes transgender dressing. Three of the thirteen states additionally bar women from posing as men.

Litigation has narrowed the state layer without loosening the federal one. A High Court request to declare the Sharia cross-dressing prohibition unconstitutional was denied, and the Federal Court struck down Selangor's section 28 in February 2021 and sixteen Kelantan Sharia provisions in February 2024, both on federalism grounds, leaving the Penal Code offences fully intact. A separate constitutional challenge was pending as of late 2014, lodged after 16 trans women were arrested at a wedding on 8 June 2014.

Enforcement against gender nonconformity is active and publicly sanctioned. In July 2020 the Religious Affairs Minister stated that the Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department (Jawi) had his full licence to carry out its enforcement actions against transgender people, an order the International Commission of Jurists demanded be revoked. In the case of the prominent transgender woman Nur Sajat, 122 religious officers were mobilised on charges of 'insulting Islam' before she fled to Thailand and received UNHCR protection. Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters documented in August 2022 that conversion and rehabilitation programmes, event shutdowns and pervasive official antipathy shape law enforcement, judicial outcomes and public discourse.

Raids on venues carry the sharpest exposure risk for foreign visitors. On 28 November 2025 police raided a male-only sauna in Chow Kit, Kuala Lumpur, arresting 208 men under section 377B, the largest operation of its kind since 2022. Media had been pre-notified and detainees' faces and personal details were published; 17 civil servants identified among them were suspended. A magistrate rejected the remand extension as lacking ground, yet release was delayed, with more than 130 people held at one point, among them 31 foreign nationals whose embassies intervened. Justice For Sisters mobilised bailors and legal aid. On 2 December the Home Minister floated revisiting the provisions, and days later police raided another sauna in Penang.

Trans women in Malaysia face lethal violence alongside official indifference. A transgender woman was killed in Klang on 25 June 2019, the third killing of a trans woman in the country in under two months; documentation of that case records police mistreatment and impunity under the heading 'The Deceased Can't Speak for Herself'. The Human Dignity Trust records consistent reports of discrimination and violence, with transgender people particularly exposed to physical and verbal abuse, and notes a crackdown on LGBT people following the 2018 election.

The wider climate is one of state-backed restriction. Government-funded mukhayyam 'rehabilitation' retreats had drawn 1,733 attendees by June 2021, LGBT events and media content are censored, Islamist opposition has foreclosed reform, and there is no same-sex marriage and no anti-discrimination law.

For a non-Muslim foreign visitor, the Sharia cross-dressing offences do not apply, but the Penal Code does. Enforcement against consenting adults in private is uncommon and tourists are rarely singled out; the documented pattern is raid-based arrest followed by public exposure rather than individual stops.
tangentialFactors:
The federalism rulings affect neighbouring states rather than Malacca directly. The Federal Court's February 2021 decision on Selangor's section 28 and its February 2024 decision on sixteen Kelantan provisions rested on the distribution of legislative powers between federal and state lists, a reasoning that leaves Malacca's own cross-dressing enactment and the federal Penal Code offences untouched.

Recent raid activity has concentrated in Kuala Lumpur and Penang rather than Malacca, which is relevant to how visitors plan movement: the documented 2025 operations targeted male-only venues in the national capital and, within days, in Penang. Foreign nationals held in the Chow Kit operation were released only after their embassies intervened, indicating that consular contact is a practical lever in detention.

Public exposure is part of the enforcement mechanism. Pre-notified media coverage of the November 2025 raid, publication of detainees' faces and details, and the suspension of 17 identified civil servants show that arrest carries occupational and social consequences beyond the legal penalty. The Nur Sajat prosecution followed a similar trajectory, escalating from religious-department pursuit to flight abroad and UNHCR protection.

Comparatively, three of Malaysia's thirteen states criminalise women posing as men as well as men posing as women, so the direction of gender nonconformity policed varies between states. Malacca's own drafting in this respect is not separately sourced here.
localsOnly:
Malaysians who are Muslim in Malacca are exposed to both layers at once: the federal Penal Code offences and the state Sharia cross-dressing enactment, the latter carrying up to three years' imprisonment, an RM5,000 fine and six strokes of caning and enforced by the state Islamic religious department. Non-Muslim residents are reached only by the Penal Code.

Government-funded mukhayyam 'rehabilitation' retreats are a resident-facing programme, with 1,733 attendees recorded by June 2021. Human Rights Watch and Justice for Sisters describe such conversion and rehabilitation programmes, together with event shutdowns, as a recurring feature of official policy rather than isolated incidents.

Residents face documented discrimination and violence in employment, family life and encounters with police, and the Human Dignity Trust records transgender people as particularly vulnerable to physical and verbal abuse. The 2019 Klang killing and the documented police mistreatment in that case indicate that complaints of violence may not be pursued.

Marriage to a same-sex partner is not recognised, and no anti-discrimination statute protects sexual orientation or gender identity at either federal or state level.
outOfScopeNotes:
Malacca-specific enforcement data is unresolved. The inventory carries no arrest, raid or caning figures for the state of Malacca itself; the recent documented operations are in Kuala Lumpur and Penang, and the national pattern is used here as the basis for expectations in Malacca.

Whether Malacca's Sharia enactment also bars women from posing as men is not sourced. Three of the thirteen states are recorded as doing so, but which three is not stated.

The status of the constitutional challenge filed after the 8 June 2014 mass arrest of 16 trans women is unresolved beyond the record that it was pending as of late 2014; no outcome is sourced.

The application of section 377D, outrages on decency, specifically against a foreign visitor in Malacca is not documented here. The Human Dignity Trust records the provision's terms as usable against transgender people, but no case involving a non-resident is cited.
